failure_summary.description: Selected stronger or weaker conclusions by analogy or plausibility instead of verifying every part of the stated classification.
Added an unstated converse or premise, or failed to distinguish a universal claim from a conditional characterization.
Confused close alternatives differing in an exponent or sign convention.
Treated linked parameters as independent and incorrectly accepted an edge case without applying all hypotheses.

patch.reasoning: The recurring issue is evaluating plausible mathematical claims rather than matching each option to the exact scope and hypotheses. Add explicit checks for unstated premises, linked parameter constraints, and every conjunct of the claimed conclusion. The annuity exponent distinction is already recorded in the skill, so it is not repeated here.

edits.content: **Separate assumptions from conclusions.** Translate the prompt and each option into explicit quantifiers before deciding. Do not silently assume a property (such as invariance) that the prompt does not grant; a conditional or equivalence may be true yet fail to answer a universal claim. Treat added converses such as “every admissible parameter occurs” as separate claims requiring support.

**Do not transfer familiar theorems to specialized notions.** A modified derivative or named geometric object need not obey the standard conclusion suggested by its name. Distinguish a linearized solution or kernel element from an integrable deformation, and verify polynomial and characteristic-class conventions before deciding signs. Small-case checks can expose errors but do not establish a general identity.

**Apply linked hypotheses before testing edge cases.** When the prompt gives an equation relating parameters, derive the consequences of that relation before treating their values as independent. Check equality and strict-inequality cases, endpoint values, and the scope of any “otherwise” clause; do not reject a boundary case merely because it seems possible in isolation.

**Compare the full strength of each option, clause by clause.** Check exact asymptotics against big-O bounds, one-sided against two-sided estimates, exact parameter values against inequalities, and fixed objects against parameter-dependent ones. Do not settle for a trivially true weaker option when a stronger one is supported, and do not accept or reject a stronger option based only on plausibility—verify its entire claim.
